home.intro: Follow the missionary journeys across the ancient Mediterranean — every place, date and claim is cited, and contested points are shown as such.

sourcing.title: How we source
sourcing.body: Dates are shown as scholarly ranges, not single years. Each claim carries citations and a confidence level. Tertiary sources — Wikipedia, popular encyclopedias, study-Bible maps, devotional sites — are only ever orienting links, never the sole authority: every claim is also backed by a concrete source (a primary text, a standard scholarly work, an excavation report, or a gazetteer), and the content build blocks any claim that rests on tertiary sources alone. High-confidence coordinates must additionally carry a place-specific citation or a Pleiades gazetteer id — a whole-atlas reference is not enough. Ambiguous locations show their rival candidates rather than a single false pin, and route strokes are drawn by geometry grade so a surveyed Roman road never looks like a schematic connector. Where scholars or traditions disagree, we say so. Bible text is public domain (King James Version, American Standard Version). This atlas is carefully cited and reviewed — it does not claim to be definitive.
